articleTitle: Application of systems identification techniques to a superheater simulator using MATLAB
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Aided Control System Design Algorithms and Packages for Personal Computers
abstract: The CEGB has devised a distributed computer installation consisting of a host machine and three target machines. One target controls five real and simulated plant systems via a suitable interface. The five plants have been selected to demonstrate different aspects of control such as three-element, cascade and ratio. The plant was designed as scaled down versions of boiler drums, temperature controllers, pressure systems, etc., and has been constructed as working engineering systems using hardware such as motors, valves, water tanks and pipework. Each physical plant system may be controlled by a target computer running CUTLASS software schemes. In order to give more of the CEGB trainee engineers hands on experience of real-time control using CUTLASS, the development of a low cost version of the power plant simulator was proposed. The low cost simulator is able to simulate any of the original sections of plant, or several sections simultaneously by using a dedicated microprocessor.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: PC based CACSD software-future developments-a tour of the horizon
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Aided Control System Design Algorithms and Packages for Personal Computers
abstract: In control engineering it is now evident that the availability and propagation of computer aided control systems design (CACSD) software has had two profound effects: it has helped in the understanding and the teaching of the subject, and it has led to the rapid spread of new techniques. The author paints a picture of the hardware and software tools that will become available to control engineers over the next decade, based on what is available today. It is safe to predict that equipment will get faster, cheaper and bigger. It is also safe to predict that the production of CACSD software and its use will get easier and quicker as the software tools are developed. What is distressing however is that the software foundations for these tools were laid ten years ago or more. For example, the popular icon based interfaces of today were conceived as part of the Dynabook project at Xerox, which began in 1960. To take a more exciting (and risky) prediction, look to the development of object oriented hardware to support directly the software concepts that have now been around for a decade and which offer the most hope for the development of software in the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A teaching interface for use with PC MATLAB
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Aided Control System Design Algorithms and Packages for Personal Computers
abstract: A brief description is given of a menu interface written for PC-MATLAB for studying a simple single-input single-output feedback system. Since the user requires no knowledge of PC-MATLAB commands it is extremely helpful both for use in teaching a first course on control systems or for the industrial user who makes infrequent use of computer aided design software.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Aided Control System Design Algorithms and Packages for Personal Computers
abstract: There are at least a dozen commercial offerings of interactive PC-based software for computer-aided control system design (CACSD). The CACSD scene has been totally transformed by these developments. It is now possible for any control engineering team to be well equipped with up to date algorithms at very modest cost, to be able to tailor them to its own requirements, and to interface them easily to other software. One of the most important effects of this has been the rapid transfer of technology from academic research to usable software. After remarking briefly on these general points, the author concentrates on a particular family of products based on PC-Matlab.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SIMBOL2-the block diagram approach to simulation, analysis and design of mixed digital, nonlinear and continuous systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Aided Control System Design Algorithms and Packages for Personal Computers
abstract: SIMBOL2 provides free form and interactive block diagram entry and editing of system specifications, by careful choice of algorithms allowing continuous, digital and nonlinear elements to be mixed freely and by providing a fully menu driven environment with context sensitive help system running on an IBM PC, AT or PS2. These features are illustrated in the context of a typical industrial control system design. The system chosen is a digital idle control system for high speed diesel engines. The model contains time delays, discrete microprocessor control, engine inertia, and nonlinear torque characteristics. Simulated and actual performance are compared, and a predicted limit cycle confirmed. The advantages of the SIMBOL2 approach to analysis and design of practical industrial systems can be seen from the example.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
